idiom_name: Unexported struct fields with exported accessor methods
implementation_notes: Go's encapsulation boundary is the package, not the type: a struct whose field names are lowercase cannot be read or written from another package, and exported methods with a value or pointer receiver are the only read path - so the classic Target/Data split collapses into one struct with unexported fields plus accessors, constructed through a `NewX` function. True immutability is not expressible: code in the same package can still assign the fields, reflection can read them, and an accessor that returns a slice or map hands out a writable reference, so pair the idiom with defensive copies and documented conventions. Keep a small unexported holder struct inside the exported type when several fields form one invariant that must be validated and copied together.
pitfalls: An accessor returning `[]T` or `map[K]V` leaks a writable reference to the 'read-only' state; return a copy or a documented read-only view.
The boundary is the package, not the type: any file in the same package can assign unexported fields, and `encoding/json` plus reflection still read them, so keep invariant enforcement in one place.
Copying the holder copies its fields but shares any pointers, slices or maps inside it, so value semantics do not give deep immutability.
